screens.title: Bitcoin Transactions Explained
screens.subtitle: How UTXOs, inputs, outputs, fees and signatures form every transfer

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how Bitcoin represents value as discrete coins called unspent transaction outputs, or UTXOs, and how transactions consume those coins and create new ones. We will use a cash-wallet analogy so you can visualize inputs as bills you hand over, outputs as new bills created, and change as the bill returned to you. Understanding this model is essential because it is the foundation of how Bitcoin records ownership without account balances. You will also see why transaction fees exist, how they are computed as inputs minus outputs, and why digital signatures are used to authorize each spent UTXO. Along the way I’ll point out common beginner mistakes, like forgetting a change output or miscalculating fees. By the end you’ll be able to deconstruct a real transaction and answer why a transaction with two small inputs often costs more to confirm than one with a single large input. Keep this mental model of bills and change; it will make the technical details feel intuitive.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Bitcoin moves value by consuming prior outputs (UTXOs) as inputs and creating new outputs. Fees and signatures secure and prioritize those transfers.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll learn and how you'll demonstrate it

narration.text: In this section we set clear learning targets so you know what mastery looks like. First, you will deconstruct the parts of a Bitcoin transaction: inputs, outputs, version and locktime, and how they combine to form a new ledger entry. Practically, this means being able to point at an explorer entry and say which fields are inputs and which are outputs. Second, you will explain the UTXO model: why Bitcoin tracks discrete unspent outputs rather than account balances, and how wallets aggregate UTXOs into a displayed balance. Third, you will describe how digital signatures authorize spending and why the private key must remain secret. Finally, you will identify common mistakes like omitting a change output or underestimating the fee. Each objective ties to a competency milestone so you can verify understanding by examining a real transaction and computing fee and change.

screens.title: UTXO model — the atomic unit of Bitcoin
screens.subtitle: Why Bitcoin tracks unspent outputs, not account balances

narration.text: Start by imagining your physical wallet full of separate bills and coins. Each bill is a distinct spendable unit. Bitcoin models value the same way: each incoming payment creates one or more unspent transaction outputs, or UTXOs, and those UTXOs are the only things that can be spent later. This definition matters because when a wallet shows a single balance it is only aggregating many discrete UTXOs for convenience. The operational implication is that spending requires selecting specific UTXOs as inputs, which are then entirely consumed. For example, if you have a 0.5 BTC UTXO and a 0.3 BTC UTXO and you want to pay 0.6 BTC, your wallet will typically select both UTXOs, consuming 0.8 BTC in inputs. If you don’t create a change output for the leftover 0.2 BTC, that leftover is treated as extra fee and goes to miners. A common misconception is to think of transactions simply as balance transfers; instead a transaction is a set of inputs referencing prior outputs and a set of newly created outputs. The takeaway: think in terms of coins you hold and spend, not a mutable account balance.

keyIdea.title: UTXO definition
keyIdea.text: A UTXO is a discrete, spendable output created by a transaction. Wallets aggregate UTXOs but spending consumes them individually.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › UTXO model — the atomic unit of Bitcoin
UTXO — definition and metaphor
A UTXO is an amount of Bitcoin created by a prior transaction and not yet spent. Wallets show totals by summing UTXOs you control.
Metaphor: cash bills
  • Each UTXO is like a separate bill in your wallet.
  • Spending consumes whole bills; change recreates a bill to you.
  • Wallet totals are the sum of your bills, not a single mutable balance.
Key Takeaway

Think coins, not accounts. Each UTXO is consumed when spent and becomes history in the chain of transactions.

Scenario
You received a 0.5 BTC payment and a 0.3 BTC payment. Your wallet shows 0.8 BTC. If you send 0.6 BTC, which UTXOs are consumed and what happens to the remainder?
Inputs selected
0.5 BTC + 0.3 BTC = 0.8 BTC consumed
Outputs created
0.6 BTC to recipient, 0.2 BTC to your change address (unless omitted)
A common misconception is to treat UTXOs like an account you can partially spend. Remember: inputs are fully consumed. Any remainder must be explicitly returned as change.
Check your understanding
If you only choose the 0.5 BTC UTXO for a 0.3 BTC payment and omit change, what happens to the 0.2 BTC difference?

screens.title: Inputs and Outputs — how a transaction is formed
screens.subtitle: The lifecycle: reference, consume, create

narration.text: A Bitcoin transaction is a statement that consumes previous outputs and creates new outputs. The process begins when your wallet selects one or more UTXOs as inputs. Each input contains a reference to the previous transaction's ID and the specific output index being spent. Those inputs are entirely consumed when the transaction is confirmed. Next, the transaction defines outputs: one or more new UTXOs that specify a value and a script determining who can spend them. The sum of input values must equal the sum of output values plus the fee. If inputs are larger than the payment, the excess becomes a change output returning coins to the sender. Conceptually, think: reference the bill, sign it to permit spending, then create new bills for the recipient and for change. A common mistake is forgetting to add a change output; that omission effectively gives the remainder to miners as a higher fee. Practice by tracing a simple transaction with two inputs and two outputs to see each field's role. Inputs and Outputs — how a transaction is formed means inputs reference and consume prior utxos; outputs create new utxos. fee = sum(inputs) − sum(outputs).. In practical terms, the lifecycle: reference, consume, create. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transaction lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Inputs reference and consume prior UTXOs; outputs create new UTXOs. Fee = sum(inputs) − sum(outputs).

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Inputs and Outputs — how a transaction is formed
Transaction process
Follow these steps when forming a transaction.
  1. Select inputs. Wallet chooses UTXOs to cover amount plus fee.
  2. Build outputs. One output to recipient, optional change output back to sender.
  3. Calculate fee. Inputs − outputs equals miner fee.
  4. Sign inputs. Sign each input with the corresponding private key.
Note: More inputs increases transaction size in bytes, which often raises the fee required for timely confirmation.
Example
Inputs: 0.7 BTC and 0.4 BTC. Outputs: 0.9 BTC to friend, 0.1999 BTC change. Fee: 0.0001 BTC. The inputs reference previous TxIDs and specific output indexes.
Why inputs matter
They prove which previous outputs are being spent and determine the total available value.
Why outputs matter
They set the new ownership and are the UTXOs future transactions will reference.
Common mistake

Omitting a change output sends the leftover as an implicit fee. Always confirm outputs equal the intended recipient and change sums.

screens.title: Change outputs vs burning as fees
screens.subtitle: Why explicit change is important and the cost of omission

narration.text: When your inputs exceed the amount you intend to send, the leftover can either be returned to you as a change output or implicitly given to miners as an extra fee. Creating an explicit change output makes ownership clear and preserves your remaining funds. If you forget the change output, the leftover disappears from your wallet balance because miners claim it as part of the fee. The practical difference is financial and privacy-related: an explicit change output creates a new UTXO you control, which can be spent later, while omission results in an irreversible transfer of value to miners. Some users think omitting change is a harmless shortcut; it is not. You would permanently lose the remainder. Another misconception is that change outputs always reuse your address — modern wallets often create a new change address for privacy. So check both the amounts and the addresses when constructing a transaction to ensure the intended remainder returns to you. Change outputs vs burning as fees means explicit change returns leftover value to the sender as a new utxo; omission converts leftover into miner fees and permanently removes the value from your wallet.. In practical terms, why explicit change is important and the cost of omission. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Change vs fee
keyIdea.text: Explicit change returns leftover value to the sender as a new UTXO; omission converts leftover into miner fees and permanently removes the value from your wallet.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Change outputs vs burning as fees
Compare outcomes
Two paths when inputs exceed payment: create change or leave none and increase fee.
Explicit Change Output
  • Creates a new UTXO controlled by you.
  • Preserves leftover value for future spending.
  • Often uses a fresh change address for privacy.
No Change (Implicit Fee)
  • Leftover is claimed by miner as additional fee.
  • Value is permanently gone from your wallet.
  • May be costly if omission was accidental.
Concrete example
Inputs: 0.8 BTC. Intended payment: 0.6 BTC. If you create change: output to recipient 0.6 BTC, change 0.1999 BTC, fee 0.0001 BTC. If you forget change: output to recipient 0.6 BTC, fee becomes 0.199999 BTC and you lose the remainder.
A useful check: always compute inputs − outputs and verify it matches the fee you intend to pay. If it’s larger than expected, you probably forgot a change output.
Pro tip
Inspect the recipient and change addresses. If both outputs look unfamiliar, confirm which one is your change before broadcasting.

screens.title: Transaction fees — calculation and incentives
screens.subtitle: How fees are determined and why they matter to miners

narration.text: Transaction fee is the economic incentive that motivates miners to include your transaction in a block. It is computed simply as the sum of input values minus the sum of output values. Fees are not fixed; they vary with network demand and transaction size measured in bytes. More inputs usually means a larger byte size, so using many small UTXOs can increase the fee needed for timely confirmation. Miners prioritize transactions with higher fee per byte, so a large absolute fee paid by a huge transaction may be less competitive than a smaller fee on a compact transaction if the fee per byte is lower. A practical example: spending two small inputs to send a small payment often costs more than spending a single larger input. A common misconception is thinking total BTC amount alone determines priority; the key metric is fee per byte. When constructing transactions, wallets typically suggest a fee rate based on current network conditions. The takeaway: be mindful of UTXO fragmentation and fee rate when planning spending. Transaction fees — calculation and incentives means transaction fee = total inputs − total outputs. miners rank by fee per byte, not total fee alone.. In practical terms, how fees are determined and why they matter to miners. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fee formula
keyIdea.text: Transaction fee = total inputs − total outputs. Miners rank by fee per byte, not total fee alone.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Transaction fees — calculation and incentives
Fee mechanics
Fee = sum(inputs) − sum(outputs). Miners prefer transactions offering higher fee per byte.
Why size matters
Each input and output adds bytes. More inputs means a larger transaction, increasing the fee needed to reach a given fee per byte.
Practical effect
If you consolidate many small UTXOs during low-fee periods, future transactions will be cheaper. If you spend many fragments during peak times, expect higher fees.
Concrete calculation
Inputs: 1.1 BTC total. Outputs: 0.9001 BTC total. Fee = 0.1999 BTC. Compare fee per byte to current network rates to estimate inclusion probability.
Misconception check
Paying a larger total fee does not guarantee faster confirmation if the fee per byte is low. Miners rank by fee density, so compact transactions with higher density get priority.
Try this
Use a wallet's fee estimator and compare the suggested fee for a 1-input versus a 3-input transaction paying the same amount. Notice the difference.

screens.title: Digital Signatures and authorization
screens.subtitle: How ECDSA proves ownership without revealing private keys

narration.text: Digital signatures are the cryptographic proof that a spender controls the private key associated with the UTXO they wish to spend. Bitcoin commonly uses the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm. When you sign, your wallet creates a unique signature for each input that can be verified by anyone holding the corresponding public key or public key hash. The signature does not reveal the private key; it only proves authorization over the specific transaction data. If a signature is missing or invalid the network rejects the transaction as unauthorized. A common student confusion is believing that signatures encrypt the transaction; they do not. Signatures authenticate and authorize; they do not hide data. Another important point: each input requires its own valid signature. This is why spending multiple UTXOs means producing multiple signatures, one per input. The practical takeaway: keep your private key secure, and understand that signatures are the permission slip that allows miners and nodes to accept the spending of a UTXO. Digital Signatures and authorization means signatures authenticate ownership for each input. they allow verification without exposing private keys.. In practical terms, how ecdsa proves ownership without revealing private keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Signature role
keyIdea.text: Signatures authenticate ownership for each input. They allow verification without exposing private keys.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Digital Signatures and authorization
Signatures — what they do
A signature proves that the spender controls the private key tied to the UTXO without revealing the key itself.
One signature per input. Each consumed UTXO requires an authorization signature.
Verification is public. Any node can verify the signature using the public key.
Not encryption. Signatures prove permission; they do not hide transaction contents.
Concrete example
If you spend two inputs, the transaction will include two script_signatures. Each script_signature contains the signature and public key data required to unlock its referenced UTXO.
Misconception
Some learners think a single signature covers the whole transaction. In Bitcoin, each input generally has its own signature that references the input’s unlocking script.
Why this matters
Signatures prevent unauthorized spending. If private keys are leaked, signatures can be forged and funds lost, which is why key security is paramount.

screens.title: Transaction structure — conceptual JSON walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Understanding fields: version, locktime, inputs, outputs, scripts

narration.text: Here we examine a simplified transaction representation to make the structure concrete. A transaction has a version and optional locktime for timing rules. The inputs array lists the previous transaction IDs and output indexes being spent, plus the signature script and sequence. The outputs array lists destination scripts and values in satoshis. Every input's script_signature is the digital signature and associated public key material that unlocks the referenced UTXO. Inspecting a block explorer, you will see these same elements presented in a human-friendly way. Review the JSON snippet on the screen and notice how inputs reference prior transactions by ID and index. The practical exercise is to take a real explorer entry and map each displayed input and output field to the JSON keys shown here. A common confusion is reading script fields as opaque; while they look technical, they are simply the locking and unlocking conditions expressed in Bitcoin script. Your goal is to map explorer fields to the JSON structure and compute fee from the numeric values. }
Mapping exercise
Take a transaction from an explorer and find: transaction_id, each input's previous_transaction_id and output_index, each output's value and script_pubkey. Then compute fee by summing inputs and outputs.
Key Takeaway

The JSON is just a compact map of fields you can see in explorers. Practice mapping to build fluency.

Misconception
Script fields look complex but are only the locking conditions and signatures; you do not need to read every opcode to compute fees or identify inputs/outputs.

screens.title: Wallet coin selection and input choices
screens.subtitle: How wallets pick UTXOs and why it affects cost and privacy

narration.text: Wallets implement coin selection algorithms to choose which UTXOs to use as inputs for a transaction. Simple strategies pick the smallest combination that covers the payment and fee, while other strategies try to minimize change or avoid creating dust. The chosen inputs affect both fee and privacy. Using many small UTXOs increases transaction size and therefore fee; using a single large UTXO is cheaper to spend but may reduce privacy if it links previously separate coins. Wallets sometimes consolidate UTXOs in a separate transaction during low-fee periods to reduce future costs. Another practical consideration is address reuse: many wallets generate a new change address, which helps unlink transactions but requires careful tracking of UTXOs across addresses. A common misunderstanding is assuming the wallet always optimizes fees; in practice wallets balance fee, privacy, and UTXO management policies. Understanding coin selection helps you plan when to consolidate or when to spend specific UTXOs to manage fees and privacy trade-offs. Wallet coin selection and input choices means coin selection balances fee, privacy, and utxo management. many small inputs increase costs; consolidation can reduce future fees.. In practical terms, how wallets pick utxos and why it affects cost and privacy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Coin selection
keyIdea.text: Coin selection balances fee, privacy, and UTXO management. Many small inputs increase costs; consolidation can reduce future fees.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Wallet coin selection and input choices
Coin selection strategies
Different wallets use different heuristics: minimize fee, minimize change, preserve privacy, or compact many UTXOs offline.
Greedy: pick smallest number of UTXOs totaling at least the payment.
Branch and bound: search for an exact match to avoid change.
Privacy-aware: avoid combining UTXOs that would link unrelated funds.
Concrete trade-offs
  • Many small inputs → larger byte size → higher fee.
  • Consolidation reduces fee later but costs a fee now.
  • Using a large input may reveal linkages across payments.
Assess your priorities: limit fees, maintain privacy, or reduce UTXO fragmentation. Wallets make trade-offs for you, but understanding them helps you choose when to consolidate or which UTXOs to spend.
Pro tip
If you have many tiny UTXOs, consider consolidating during a low-fee window to lower long-term costs.

screens.title: Deconstructing a real transaction (guided)
screens.subtitle: Walkthrough steps to inspect inputs, outputs, and fee in an explorer

narration.text: This guided activity shows how to deconstruct a real, simple transaction. First, pick a recent transaction with one or two inputs and two outputs. Note the transaction ID. Next, open the inputs section and for each input record the previous TxID and the output index, and the value spent from that UTXO. Then open the outputs section and list each recipient script and its value. Sum all input values and all output values. Subtract outputs from inputs to compute the fee. Compare your computed fee to the explorer’s reported fee; they should match. Identify which output is likely change by comparing address patterns and amounts. If both outputs go to different addresses, the smaller one is often the change, but wallets vary. A common error students make is misreading satoshis vs BTC; remember to convert units or compute entirely in satoshis to avoid rounding mistakes. This activity trains you to map explorer data into the transaction structure and verify fees by hand. Deconstructing a real transaction (guided) means practice mapping explorer fields to transaction inputs, outputs, and fee by computing sums and identifying change output.. In practical terms, walkthrough steps to inspect inputs, outputs, and fee in an explorer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Guided deconstruction
keyIdea.text: Practice mapping explorer fields to transaction inputs, outputs, and fee by computing sums and identifying change output.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Deconstructing a real transaction (guided)
Step-by-step walkthrough
  1. Choose a recent simple transaction (1–2 inputs, 2 outputs).
  2. Record the Transaction ID (TxID).
  3. For each input: note previous TxID, output index, and value in satoshis.
  4. For each output: note script type or address and value in satoshis.
  5. Sum inputs and outputs; compute fee = inputs − outputs and verify with explorer.
  6. Identify likely change output and explain your reasoning.
Unit clarity
Work in satoshis for exact arithmetic. 1 BTC = 100,000,000 satoshis. Converting mid-calculation can introduce rounding errors.
Check your understanding
After deconstruction, can you explain where each input came from and which output will be spent next by the sender?
Common error
Mixing BTC and satoshi units. Always compute fees using the same unit to avoid mistakes.

screens.title: Common mistakes when constructing transactions
screens.subtitle: Practical pitfalls: omitted change, insufficient fee, unit confusion

narration.text: Learners commonly make a small set of avoidable mistakes when building transactions. First, forgetting a change output causes the remainder to be claimed as a fee. That error is costly but easy to catch by calculating inputs minus outputs before broadcasting. Second, underestimating the fee or ignoring fee per byte leads to long confirmation delays; always check fee rate, not just absolute fee. Third, unit confusion between BTC and satoshis causes arithmetic mistakes; convert to satoshis or stick with one unit throughout. Fourth, attempting to reuse addresses or blindly consolidating UTXOs can harm privacy. Finally, assuming a single signature covers multiple inputs is incorrect: each input needs an appropriate signature. To avoid these problems, practice the deconstruction exercise, use wallet fee estimators, and inspect the raw transaction fields before signing. These habits reduce the chance of losing funds or waiting unexpectedly long for confirmation. Common mistakes when constructing transactions means calculate inputs − outputs, check fee per byte, use consistent units, and ensure change outputs and signatures are correct before broadcasting.. In practical terms, practical pitfalls: omitted change, insufficient fee, unit confusion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoidable pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Calculate inputs − outputs, check fee per byte, use consistent units, and ensure change outputs and signatures are correct before broadcasting.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Common mistakes when constructing transactions
Top mistakes and fixes
  • Omitted change: compute inputs − outputs before signing.
  • Insufficient fee: check suggested fee per byte against network conditions.
  • Unit confusion: use satoshis for exact arithmetic.
  • Privacy leak: avoid combining unrelated UTXOs unless necessary.
  • Signature misunderstandings: each input needs a valid signature.
Example fix
Before broadcasting, list inputs and outputs in satoshis: if inputs total 1,100,000 satoshis and outputs total 900,100 satoshis, fee is 199,900 satoshis. If you expected a smaller fee, check whether change was omitted.
Quick checklist
Verify signatures present, verify change exists if expected, confirm fee per byte, and use consistent units.
Reflection
Which of these mistakes have you seen in explorers or wallets? Practicing the guided walkthrough builds habits to prevent them.

screens.title: Practice assessment — UTXO calculation problems
screens.subtitle: Sample questions and worked solutions to test mastery

narration.text: Here are two short assessment problems you can practice to test your understanding. Problem one: you have UTXOs 0.7 BTC and 0.4 BTC and want to send 0.9 BTC with a network fee of 0.0001 BTC. Calculate the change and list inputs and outputs. Walk through the math in satoshis to avoid rounding. Problem two: explain the primary purpose of a digital signature in a Bitcoin transaction. For the first problem, convert to satoshis: 0.7 is 70,000,000 and 0.4 is 40,000,000. Combined inputs equal 110,000,000 satoshis. The amount to send plus fee is 90,000,000 + 10,000 = 90,010,000 satoshis. Change equals 19,990,000 satoshis or 0.1999 BTC. The transaction likely has two inputs and two outputs. For the second problem, the correct explanation is that a digital signature cryptographically proves authorization to spend the referenced UTXO without revealing the private key. Practicing these problems helps you quickly reason about real transactions on explorers. Inputs total = 110,000,000 satoshis
Send = 0.9 BTC = 90,000,000 satoshis
Fee = 0.0001 BTC = 10,000 satoshis
Change = Inputs - Send - Fee = 110,000,000 - 90,000,000 - 10,000 = 19,990,000 satoshis = 0.1999 BTC
Transaction: 2 inputs, 2 outputs (recipient + change)
Problem 2 (explain)
What is the primary purpose of a digital signature in a Bitcoin transaction?
Answer: A digital signature proves that the sender controls the private key associated with the UTXO being spent, authorizing the transfer without revealing the private key itself.
Key takeaway
Solving calculation problems in satoshis and explaining signature purpose demonstrates both numeric fluency and conceptual understanding.

narration.text: This quick summary captures three essential definitions to carry forward. First, a UTXO is a discrete, unspent output — the atomic unit of Bitcoin’s accounting model. It is created by an output in a transaction and can only be spent once. Second, a transaction input is a reference to a previous UTXO and includes the unlocking data, typically a digital signature, proving authorization. Third, a transaction output defines a new UTXO with a value and the script specifying who may spend it next. Knowing these definitions helps you read any transaction and reason about value flow on the network. Use this as a mental checklist when inspecting transactions: where did the coins come from, what authorizes spending, and who will control the outputs created? Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Key Concepts — What to Remember (1/2)
Unspent Transaction Output (UTXO)
An output that has been received and not yet spent. The atomic unit wallets manage.
Transaction Input
Reference to a prior UTXO plus unlocking data (signature) that authorizes spending.
Transaction Output
A new UTXO specifying value and a script that defines who can spend it next.
Summary takeaway
Read transactions as a flow of discrete coins: inputs consume prior outputs, outputs create new coins, and signatures and fees govern authorization and inclusion in a block.

screens.subtitle: Change outputs, fees, and digital signatures

narration.text: Finish with three more compact reminders. Change outputs return leftover value to the sender as a new UTXO; omitting change converts leftover into miner fees and permanently removes value from your wallet. Transaction fees are computed as sum(inputs) minus sum(outputs) and miners prioritize transactions by fee per byte. Digital signatures authorize each input and prove control of the private key without revealing it. These three points connect operation, economics, and security. When you inspect a transaction, compute inputs minus outputs to verify the fee, look for a change output to ensure you keep the remainder, and confirm that each input includes an unlocking signature. Master these checks and you'll reliably interpret and evaluate basic Bitcoin transactions. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Key Concepts — What to Remember (2/2)
Change Output
An output returning leftover value to the sender as a new UTXO; omission increases fee.
Transaction Fee
Calculated as total inputs minus total outputs. Miners prefer higher fee per byte for inclusion priority.
Digital Signature (ECDSA)
Cryptographic proof that the transaction spender controls the private key and is authorized to spend each input.
Final takeaway
When inspecting or constructing transactions, compute fees, confirm change, and verify signatures to ensure correct, authorized transfers of value.
